name: Kamarupa period
summary: The Varman, Salastambha and Pala dynasties of ancient Kamarupa, ruling most of the Brahmaputra valley.
group_order: Barman dynasty; Salastambha dynasty; Pala dynasty; Contemporaries and visitors

name: Western (Namoni) Assam after 1100
summary: The kingdoms of Lower (Namoni) Assam and north Bengal after the Palas: the successors of Kamarupa, Kamata, the Khen and Bhuyan rulers, and the Koch kingdom with its branches Koch Hajo, Koch Bihar, Darrang, Beltola, Bijni and Khaspur. Sultans from Bengal and Delhi raided this region from 1206.
group_order: Kamarupa after the Palas; Pala Empire of Bengal; Kamata and Khen kingdoms; Baro-Bhuyans; Bengal and Delhi rulers; Koch kingdom (undivided); Koch Hajo kings; Koch Bihar kings; Darrang kings; Beltola kings; Bijni kings; Khaspur kings

name: Ahom period
summary: The Tai-Ahom kingdom of Upper (Ujoni) Assam, founded by Sukaphaa in 1228 and ended by the Burmese invasions and the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826: its kings, queens, nobles and rebels, and the foreign commanders they fought.
group_order: Ahom kings; Ahom queens and royal family; Ahom officers and generals; Moamoria rebels; Mughal and Bengal commanders; Burmese and British figures

name: Neighbouring kingdoms
summary: The Chutia kingdom of Sadiya, the Dimasa (Kachari) and Barahi kingdoms of the centre and south, and Jaintia and Manipur on the edge of the hills.
group_order: Chutia kingdom; Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom; Jaintia and Manipur

name: Saints, poets and writers
summary: Assamese literature and the bhakti movement, which grew across the Kamata, Koch and Ahom lands.
group_order: Poets and writers; Saints of the bhakti movement; Legends

name: Bala Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 398–422 CE.
notes: Father of Amritaprabha, who married Meghavahana of Kashmir; Amritaprabha took Buddhist monk Stunpa with her

name: Kalyan Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 422–446 CE.
notes: Expanded territory into the Kapili valley; sent a diplomatic mission to China

name: Ganapati Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 446–470 CE.

name: Mahendra Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 470–494 CE.
notes: Kumaragupta; Skandagupta; Aswamedh jagya

name: Narayana Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 494–518 CE.

name: Bhuti Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 518–542 CE.
notes: Won over Pundravardhana; Badaganga epigraph

name: Chandramukha
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 542–566 CE.

name: Sthita Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 566–590 CE.

name: Susthita Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 590–595 CE.
notes: Mriganka; lost north Bengal to Gupta

name: Supratisthita Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 595–600 CE.
notes: Brother of Bhaskar Varman

name: Bhaskar Varman
summary: Ruler of the Barman dynasty, 600–650 CE.
notes: Ascended throne around 594 AD; alliance with Harshavardhana; campaign against Sasanka leading to capture of Gauda and Karnasuvarna; issued Nidhanpur grants reconfirming Bhutivarman land grants in Pundravardhana; hosted Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang in 642–643 AD; mentioned as Kumararaja in Chinese sources

name: Xuanzang
summary: Buddhist monk whose account of his 643 visit is a key outside description of Kamarupa.

notes: Pragjyotishpur to Tezpur or Haruppeswara / Hatakeswara

name: Avantivarman

notes: Sources disagree on the end of the dynasty (650 or 655 CE).

notes: Gaudradi-Kalinga-Kosala-pati (Pasupati epigraph); Nepal Lichvi king Jayadeva-II; Rashtrakuta king Dantidurga (Samangad epigraph)

notes: Hayunthal grant; Tezpur Rock epigraph

name: Vanamalavarmadeva
summary: Ruler of the Salastambha dynasty, 832–855 CE.
notes: Fasted unto death, evidently under the influence of religion

name: Jayamala / Virabahu
summary: Ruler of the Salastambha dynasty, 855–860 CE.
notes: Virabahu; he considered the world vain and man’s life a water-drop

summary: Ruler of the Salastambha dynasty, 890–900 CE.
notes: Brahmapala was his administrator

name: Brahma Pala
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 900–920 CE.
notes: Administrator in Salastambha and became founder of Varman dynasty

name: Ratna Pala
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 920–960 CE.
notes: Choratbari grant; Bargaon grant; Sualkuchi grant; fortified Hadapyaka (Tezpur) and renamed it Durjaya; defeated Gauda king Rajyapala

name: Indra Pala
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 960–990 CE.
notes: Guwahati grant; Guwa kuchi grant; marital relation to Rashtrakuta; held sway over Pundravardhana

name: Gopala Varman
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 990–1015 CE.
notes: His mother was a Rashtrakuta princess named Rajyadevi

name: Harsha Pala
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 1015–1035 CE.
notes: Jatavarman, king of East Bengal, snatched away a part of Pundravardhana

name: Dharma Pala
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 1035–1060 CE.
notes: Khonamukhi grant; Subhankarapataka grant; Pushpabhadra grant

name: Jaya Pala
summary: Ruler of the Pala dynasty, 1075–1100 CE.
notes: Defeated by king Ramapala of Bengal; mentioned in Ramacharita by Sandhyakara Nandi; Ramapala apparently took only possessions in North Bengal and appointed Tingyadeva as ruler

name: Kharabana
summary: Listed among rulers of the southern Kamarupa (Sylhet) region; no dates or overlord are given.
notes: Sylhet is now in Bangladesh.

name: Samudrapala
summary: Listed as ruling Kamarupa proper after Jayapala; no dates or events are given.

name: Ramapala (Pala Empire of Bengal)
summary: Conquered western Kamarupa and installed Timgyadeva as governor. Sources differ on whether he took only parts of north Bengal or Kamarupa itself.
notes: Reign given as 1072–1126 or 1077–1133.

name: Timgyadeva
role: Governor and ruler of western Kamarupa
summary: Made governor of Kamarupa by Ramapala, ruling from Hamshkonchi; later rebelled and ruled independently until he was replaced.
notes: The claim that he threw off Pala rule is marked as needing a citation.

name: Bhaskara (lunar dynasty)
summary: First of a “lunar dynasty” known from one 1185 inscription; held parts of Kamrup, Darrang and Sonitpur on the north bank.
notes: No individual dates; the four rulers share the span 1120–1200.

name: Gokuladeva
summary: Listed among rulers of the southern Kamarupa (Sylhet) region; no dates or overlord are given.
notes: Sylhet is now in Bangladesh.

name: Kumarapala (Pala king of Bengal)
summary: Sent Vaidyadeva to put down Timgyadeva's rebellion in Kamarupa and kept friendly relations with him.
notes: Some accounts call him Timgyadeva's son, which looks like a mistake; he is Ramapala's son.

name: Vaidyadeva
summary: Replaced Timgyadeva under Kumarapala, then in effect created a separate kingdom after Kumarapala's death. Issued grants in the old Kamarupa style under the elephant seal and took the title Maharajadhiraja.
notes: The Kamauli plates date his fourth year while governing under Kumarapala.

name: Narayana (Sylhet)
summary: Listed among rulers of the southern Kamarupa (Sylhet) region; no dates or overlord are given.
notes: Sylhet is now in Bangladesh.

name: Rayarideva
summary: Member of the lunar dynasty of the north bank, known only from the 1185 inscription.

name: Kesavadeva
summary: Listed among rulers of the southern Kamarupa (Sylhet) region; no dates or overlord are given.
notes: Sylhet is now in Bangladesh.

name: Udayakarna
summary: Member of the lunar dynasty known from the 1185 inscription.

name: Vallabhadeva
summary: Last named lunar-dynasty ruler; the article suggests a son of his may have been the ruler in 1206.

name: Prithu
summary: Ruler of Kamarupa remembered for destroying Bakhtiyar Khalji's army in 1205–06 and for resisting Iwaz Khalji in 1226–28; one account says he was killed in a plot in 1228. Whether the Prithu of Juzjani's chronicle is this king is disputed.
notes: One list dates him 1187–1228 with a capital at Bhittargarh. Some scholars treat “Prithu” as a rebel in Awadh and credit the Kamarupa resistance to other rulers. One source suggests the name Viswasundaradeva.

name: Ikhtiyar al-Din Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji
summary: Conquered Bengal and led a failed expedition towards Tibet through Kamarupa in 1206; the retreat ended in disaster.
notes: Some accounts date an earlier attempt to 1203. The identity of the Kamarupa ruler who resisted him is disputed.

name: Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Khalji
summary: Invaded Kamarupa in 1226–27, was worsted near Nagaon and withdrew to Lakhnauti, where he was captured and killed in 1227–28 by Nasiruddin Mahmud.

name: Sandhya (Kamateswar)
summary: Founder of the Kamata kingdom. Took the throne in 1228 as a vassal of Delhi, then stopped paying tribute; captured and executed Yuzbak in 1257 and moved the capital from Kamarupanagara to Kamatapur after that.
notes: Heritage University paper gives 1228–1265. Control over lands east of the Manas was loose. The reorganisation into the Kamata state is dated c. 1250–1270.

name: Nasiruddin Mahmud
summary: Son of Iltutmish; took Bengal after Iwaz Khalji, entered Kamarupa and installed a tributary king who lost control after Nasiruddin's death in 1229.

name: Malik Ikhtiyaruddin Yuzbak Tughril Khan
summary: Invaded Kamarupa in 1257, won early successes and was then defeated by the Kamata ruler.
notes: Accounts differ on whether he was captured or killed.

name: Sindhu Rai
summary: Early Kamata ruler listed between Sandhya and Rup Narayan; no dates or events are given.
notes: Dated 1265–1285 in the Heritage University paper; no events are given.

name: Rup Narayan
summary: Early Kamata ruler; no dates or events are given.
notes: Dated 1285–1300 in the Heritage University paper.

name: Singhadhwaj
summary: Said to have founded a new ruling line by killing the Kameswar of Sandhya's line; his minister Pratapdhwaj later took power.
notes: Dated 1300–1305 in the Heritage University paper.

name: Pratapdhwaj
role: King of Kamata (minister who took the throne)
summary: Minister of Singhadhwaj who took the throne. Faced Ghiyasuddin Bahadur Shah's raid in 1321–22 with little success, and his reign overlaps the Ahom–Kamata war of about 1324.
notes: Father of Durlabhnarayan. Dates 1305–1325 appear in two king lists.

name: Ghiyasuddin Bahadur Shah
summary: Raided Kamata as far as Nagaon, meeting ineffective resistance from Pratapdhwaj and the Kacharis, but kept no territory. Killed by Muhammad Tughlaq in 1327–28.

name: Dharmanarayan
summary: Cousin of Pratapdhwaj who took power at his death; after a settlement with Durlabhnarayan he kept Rangpur and Mymensingh.
notes: Dated 1325–1330 in one list and 1330–1350 in another that seems to conflate him with Durlabhnarayan.

name: Durlabhnarayan (Kamata)
summary: Son of Pratapdhwaj who took Kamrup, Goalpara and Koch Bihar from Kamatapur. His court poets produced early Assamese literature, including Hema Saraswati and Harihara Vipra.
notes: Replaces the earlier early-14th-century guess. The catalogue ties him to the Ahom–Kamata war of c. 1324, which falls in Pratapdhwaj's reign by these dates. The chronology and extent of his rule are disputed.

name: Indranarayan
summary: Kamata king weakened by Sikandar Shah's 1357–62 invasion; some historians say he and Mahamanikya resisted Sikandar Shah around 1362. A Bhuyan then took power.
notes: Dated 1350–1365 in two lists; 1350–1385 in another.

name: Candivara (Chandibar)
summary: Said to have been a former ruler of Kannauj who fled north India; Durlabhnarayan of Kamata settled his group at Langamaguri and later Bordowa. A descendant was Srimanta Sankardev.
notes: Possibly fled after the 1353 campaign against Ilyas Shah.

name: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah
summary: His forces advanced up the Brahmaputra and occupied Kamrup, including Guwahati, before his death around November 1357.

name: Sikandar Shah of Bengal
summary: Advanced to the Kopili river, where Kamata, Bhuyan and Barahi forces fought him near Gachtal. Silver coins of 1360 carry a Kamrup mint name, but how long he held it is unclear.
notes: The outcome of the Gachtal fighting is not stated in the article.

name: Arimatta (Sasanka)
summary: A Bhuyan of Darrang who killed Indranarayan and took the Kamata throne.
notes: It is not known when Baro-Bhuyan rule began. Gajanka, Sukranka and Mriganka are listed as successors without dates.

name: Gajanka
summary: Listed as a successor of Arimatta; no dates are given.

name: Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah
summary: An inscription at Boko in Kamrup shows the Sultanate held the region for some years. The Kamata king, allied with the Ahoms by marriage, drove him back across the Karatoya.
notes: Dates are inferred from coins.

name: Rajadhara
summary: Son of Candivara; captured by the Bhutiyas, later freed, and succeeded his father as leader of the Baro-Bhuyans.

name: Sukranka
summary: Listed as a successor of Arimatta; no dates are given.

name: Mriganka (Jungal Balahu)
summary: Removed by the Khen dynasty.
notes: Also called Jungal Balahu; removed by Niladhwaj of the Khen dynasty.

name: Gandharva Raya
summary: Ancestor of Harup Narayan in the second group of Bhuyans.

name: Niladhwaj
summary: Founder of the Khen dynasty, ruling from Kamatapur (now Gosanimari) after Mriganka. An 18th-century source calls him Kanta Nath, of humble origin.
notes: Origins disputed: a local from Jambari or a migrant from Tripura, per different accounts. The page is a stub.

name: Hajo (Koch chief)
summary: Father of Hira, so maternal grandfather of Biswa Singha; a chief of Koch Hajo's ancestral line.
notes: Reign not given.

name: Chakradhwaj (Khen)
summary: Son of Niladhwaj and second Khen ruler; his son Nilambar succeeded him.

name: Hariya Mandal (Hari Das)
role: Mech chief, father of Biswa Singha
summary: Husband of Hira and father of Biswa Singha; a Mech (Bodo) chief.

name: Nilambar
summary: Last Khen king, the most powerful of his line. Expanded Kamata into Kamrup, Darrang, northern Mymensingh and parts of Cooch Behar and built roads; Husain Shah's army took Kamatapur after a long siege in 1498.
notes: Tradition says the minister Sachipatra urged the invasion after Nilambar executed his son.

name: Shamsuddin Muzaffar Shah
summary: Invaded Kamata and took parts of it, issuing coins with the title Kamata Mardan, before Husain Shah.

name: Alauddin Husain Shah
summary: Sultan of Bengal; his general Shah Ismail Ghazi took Kamatapur in 1498–99 and annexed the land up to Hajo by 1502. His son Danyal governed it until the Bhuyans overran the garrison.
notes: Sources give 1493 or 1494 as the start of his reign and 1518 or 1519 as the end.

name: Shah Ismail Ghazi
summary: Led about 24,000 men and a river flotilla to besiege and destroy Kamatapur and capture Nilambar.

name: Sachipatra
summary: In the traditional account, a minister whose son Nilambar executed for an affair with the queen; said to have urged Husain Shah to invade. Escaped and was never heard of again.
notes: Traditional, not independently documented.

name: Harup Narayan
role: Bhuyan leader and Chota Raja of Bausi
summary: Leader of the Assamese Bhuyans who overran Danyal's garrison and ended Sultanate rule about ten years after 1498, before the Koch rose.
notes: The article gives no exact dates.

name: Shahzada Danyal
role: Governor of the conquered Kamata region
summary: Husain Shah's son, made governor of the territory up to Hajo; the Bhuyans under Harup Narayan overran his garrison and ended Sultanate rule within about ten years.

name: Biswa Singha
summary: Son of Hariya Mandal and Hira. Defeated the Baro-Bhuyans and founded the Koch kingdom in Kamata; his sons Nara Narayan and Chilarai followed.
notes: Campaigns began c. 1509; coronation 1515. Sources differ on the cause of death.

name: Sisu (Sisya Singha)
summary: Brother of Biswa Singha, made yuvaraj; his descendants became the Raikut kings of Jalpaiguri.

name: Nara Narayan
summary: Took the Koch kingdom to its peak with his brother Chilarai as commander. Introduced the Narayani silver coin; Sankardev's teaching spread in his time.
notes: Infobox gives 1554–1587; text gives 1540. Died 1587 (some sources 1588).

name: Chilarai (Sukladhwaj)
summary: Third son of Biswa Singha and commander-in-chief under Nara Narayan. Led the 1562–63 invasion that forced the Treaty of Majuli; died of smallpox in 1571.
notes: Spouse: Kamalpriya.

name: Gosain Kamal (Kamal Narayan)
summary: Step-brother of Nara Narayan; built the Gohain Kamal Ali road, governed Brahmapur (Khaspur) and opened the secret road for Chilarai's invasion of 1546.
relation: Son of Biswa Singha; first governor of Khaspur (Brahmapur)

name: Raghudev
summary: Son of Chilarai; claimed the eastern Koch lands at Barnagar in 1581 and stopped paying tribute after Nara Narayan died in 1587, making the division permanent. Father of Parikshit Narayan, Man Singha and Mangaldoi (wife of Pratap Singha).
notes: Defeated a Mughal army in 1597. His daughter Mangaldoi married Pratap Singha in 1603.

name: Lakshmi Narayan
summary: First king of Koch Bihar after the split; submitted to the Mughal subahdar in 1609 and joined the 1612 Mughal attack on Koch Hajo.
notes: Other sources give 1586 for the start and 1627 for his death.

name: Udita Narayan
summary: Declared Khaspur independent of the Koch kingdom in 1590.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Man Singha (Koch Hajo prince)
summary: Son of Raghudev and brother of Parikshit Narayan.

name: Vijay Narayana
summary: Khaspur ruler; no events given.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Parikshit Narayan
summary: Eldest son of Raghudev. Defeated by Lakshmi Narayan and the Mughals in 1602 and again in 1612; he surrendered at Pandu in 1614 and was taken to Delhi. His brothers Balinarayan and Gaj Narayan fled to the Ahoms.
notes: Another source gives his death as 1616. The Koch Hajo article lists his reign as 1603–1613 but describes events in 1614.

name: Chandra Narayan (Bijit Narayan) of Bijni
summary: Son of Parikshit Narayan; the Mughals made him zamindar between the Sankosh and Manas rivers. Bijni's control is dated 1671–1864.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Balinarayan (Dharma Narayan)
summary: Fled to the Ahoms in 1613; Pratap Singha made him tributary king of Darrang (between the Barnadi and Bharali) after the 1615 victory. Fought beside the Ahoms for two decades and was killed at Singri in 1638.
notes: The article's infobox gives 1638 (1639).
relation: Son of Raghudev; brother of Parikshit

name: Gaj Narayan Dev
summary: Brother of Parikshit Narayan and Balinarayan; set up as tributary ruler of Beltola in 1615 under the Ahom Borphukan.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Bir Narayan
summary: Pleasure-loving ruler per the Cooch Behar State article.
notes: The district history page gives his death as 1632; another list gives 1627–32.

name: Pran (Prana) Narayan
summary: Reigned almost four decades, one of the longest Koch Bihar reigns before the 18th century.
notes: The district page says he reigned till 1666.

name: Dhir Narayana
summary: Khaspur ruler; no events given.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Mahendra Narayan (Darrang)
summary: Listed as Balinarayan's successor (a son, per some accounts); no dates are given.
notes: Sources conflict on the order of succession.

name: Joy Narayan
summary: Second Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Chandra Narayan (Darrang)
summary: Son of Mahendra Narayan; installed as tributary ruler after Koch princes helped the Ahoms drive out the Mughals.

name: Shivendra Narayan Dev (Beltola)
summary: Son of Gaj Narayan.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Mahendra Narayana (Khaspur)
summary: Khaspur ruler; no events given.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Moda (Madan) Narayan
summary: His officers killed Chandra Narayan around 1667; he died in 1680 without a male heir.

name: Surya Narayan (Darrang)
summary: Captured by the Mughal commander Mansur Khan in 1682, who installed his five-year-old brother; the Ahoms removed the Mughals later that year.

name: Gandharva Narayan Dev
summary: Son of Shivendra; fought with the Ahoms under Lachit Borphukan at Saraighat and was then installed as king of Beltola.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Basudev Narayan
summary: Killed in 1682 in a skirmish with his kinsman Jagna Narayan.

name: Shiv Narayan
summary: Third Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Mahendra Narayan (Koch Bihar)
summary: A minor king, great-grandson of Pran Narayan according to the district page.
notes: Not the Darrang king of the same name.

name: Indra Narayan (Darrang)
summary: A Darrang ruler installed by the Ahoms, listed after Surya Narayan in one genealogy.

name: Uttam Narayan Dev
summary: Son of Gandharva Narayan Dev.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Ranjit (Khaspur)
summary: Khaspur ruler; no events given.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Rup Narayan
summary: Reigned 21 years.

name: Bijoy Narayan
summary: Fourth Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Dhwaja Narayan Dev
summary: Son of Uttam Narayan Dev.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Nara Singha (Khaspur)
summary: Khaspur ruler; no events given.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Upendra Narayan
summary: Reigned nearly half a century; succeeded by his young son.

name: Mukunda Narayan
summary: Fifth Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Bhim Singha (Khaspur)
summary: Last Khaspur ruler; his only child, a daughter, married a Kachari prince and Khaspur merged into the Kachari kingdom in 1745.
notes: Dates only keep the order; the source gives years only for the 1590 independence and the 1745 merger.

name: Jay Narayan Dev
summary: Son of Dhwaja Narayan Dev.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Haridev Narayan
summary: Sixth Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Balit Narayan
summary: Seventh Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Devendra Narayan
summary: Installed as a boy under the guardianship of the Nazir Deo, Lalit Narayan; died in August 1765.

name: Dhairjendra (Dhairyendra) Narayan
summary: First reign under the Bhutanese ambassador Pensuthma; deposed in 1770 and abdicated after the 1774 peace between the British and Bhutan, returning in 1775.

name: Rajendra Narayan (1770–1772)
summary: Placed on the throne by Bhutan with Pensuthma as regent.

name: Lambodar Narayan Dev
date_label: signed with the East India Company, Oct 1826
summary: Son of Jay Narayan; signed an ordinance with the East India Company in October 1826 acknowledging its overlordship; married a Manipuri princess.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Dharendra Narayan
summary: Two short reigns. After the British captured the capital in 1772 and the 1774 peace with Bhutan, Dhairjendra abdicated in his favour.

name: Bijendra Narayan
summary: Reigned between Dharendra Narayan's two terms.

name: Hangsanarayan (Darrang)
summary: Executed by royal troops around the time of the Moamoria troubles; father of the rebel prince Krishnanarayan.

name: Indra Narayan (Bijni)
summary: Eighth Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Harendra Narayan
summary: Ruled for over fifty years, under regents until 1801. His reign spans the 1826 end of Ahom rule.

name: Krishnanarayan (Darrang)
summary: Rebelled in Darrang in 1791 and occupied North Guwahati with Haradatta; defeated by Captain Welsh in 1792.

name: Amrit Narayan (Bijni)
summary: Ninth Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Kumud Narayan
summary: Tenth Bijni king.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Lokpal Narayan Dev
summary: Son of Lambodar; ruled when the British reduced Beltola from a kingdom to a mouza; died in 1863.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Shivendra Narayan
notes: After the 1826 cut-off of the main research; included to complete the Koch Bihar line.

name: Jogendra Narayan
summary: Eleventh Bijni king; the capital moved from Dumuria to Jogighopa after an 1864 attack.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Narendra Narayan
notes: After the 1826 cut-off of the main research; included to complete the Koch Bihar line.

name: Nripendra Narayan
summary: Ruled 1863–1911; regents until 1883.
notes: After the 1826 cut-off of the main research; included to complete the Koch Bihar line.

name: Amrit Narayan Dev (Beltola)
summary: Elder son of Lokpal; no children.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Bhairabendra Narayan
summary: Twelfth Bijni king; the capital moved to Abhayapuri around 1897–1901.
notes: The ruler list comes from the Koch dynasty article; it gives no reign years, so dates here only keep the order.

name: Chandra Narayan Dev (Beltola)
summary: Younger son of Lokpal; died in 1910.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Rajendra Narayan Dev (Beltola)
summary: Son of Chandra; died in 1937.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Raj Rajendra Narayan II
notes: After the 1826 cut-off of the main research; included to complete the Koch Bihar line.

name: Jitendra Narayan
summary: Ruled 1913–1922; father of Gayatri Devi.
notes: After the 1826 cut-off of the main research; included to complete the Koch Bihar line.

name: Jagaddipendra Narayan
summary: Ruled 1922–1949 (the biography section gives 1970 as the end).
notes: After the 1826 cut-off of the main research; included to complete the Koch Bihar line.

name: Lakshmipriya Devi (Beltola)
summary: Wife of Rajendra; ruled 1937–1947 and died in 1991.
notes: Beltola reign years are given only for a few rulers in the source.

name: Chaolung Sukaphaa
summary: Born around 1189 in Mong Mao, he left in 1215, crossed the Patkai hills and reached Namrup in December 1228, founding the Ahom kingdom that lasted until 1826. He built Charaideo in 1253.
notes: Married daughters of the Moran chief Badaucha and the Barahi chief Thakumatha. Moved his base from 1236 (Mungklang) through Habung (1240) and Ligirigaon (1244) before Charaideo.

name: First Burhagohain (Thaomung)
summary: The Burhagohain and Borgohain offices were created by Sukaphaa. The personal names given in the project catalogue are unverified.
notes: Name “Thaomung” comes from the project catalogue only.

name: First Borgohain (Thaomung)
summary: See the first Burhagohain: the personal name is unverified.

name: Badaucha (Moran chief)
summary: A Moran chief whose daughter Sukaphaa married as part of the Ahom settlement of the Brahmaputra valley.
notes: The project catalogue spells the name Bodousa.

name: Thakumatha (Barahi chief)
summary: A Barahi chief whose daughter Sukaphaa married as part of the Ahom settlement of the Brahmaputra valley.
notes: The project catalogue spells the name Thakumtha.

name: Suteuphaa
summary: Son of Sukaphaa; died a natural death.
notes: Catalogued scenes cover the Dikhou frontier with the Kacharis and the Naga hill campaigns.

name: Subinphaa
summary: Son of Suteuphaa; set up the Satghariya Ahom group and died naturally.

name: Sukhaangphaa
summary: Son of Subinphaa. His long war with the Kamata king (from about 1324) ended in a truce sealed by marrying the Kamata princesses Rajani and Bhajani.
notes: The king list gives a natural death, but a footnote says he was deposed and executed.
fate: Natural death (a footnote says deposed and executed)

name: Rajani
summary: Daughter of the Kamata king (Kamateswar), given with her sister Bhajani to Sukhaangphaa to seal a truce. Mother of Sukhrangphaa, Sutuphaa, Tyao Khamti and Tyao Chulai.

name: Bhajani
summary: Rajani's sister, also given to Sukhaangphaa under the treaty; mother of Chao Pulai.

name: Chao Pulai
summary: Son of Sukhaangphaa and Bhajani. The project catalogue shows him meeting Kamata envoys and being made governor of Sadiya.
notes: Governor role comes from the catalogue only.

name: Sukhrangphaa
summary: Son of Sukhaangphaa; created the post of Charing Raja. His death was followed by an interregnum (1364–1369).

name: Sutuphaa
summary: Brother of Sukhrangphaa; assassinated. Another interregnum (1376–1380) followed.

name: Tyao Khamti
summary: Brother of Sutuphaa; assassinated by nobles in 1389 (a family tree gives 1387). He led an unsuccessful expedition against the Chutias.
notes: Followed by an interregnum until 1397.

name: Thao Cheoken
summary: The trader who found the young prince Sudangphaa in Habung.

name: Sudangphaa (Bamuni Konwar)
summary: Son of Tyao Khamti, raised by a Brahmin family in Habung after his mother's execution; found and enthroned at about fifteen in 1397. He introduced the Singarigharutha coronation (1403) and let Hindu rites into the court.
notes: Peace treaty fixing the Patkai boundary in 1401; capital moved to Charguwa in 1403.

name: Chaothai Khum Burhagohain
summary: Brought the young Sudangphaa to Charaideo and enthroned him in 1397.

name: Tai Sulai
summary: A rival claimant to the Ahom throne who fled to Mungkang and gained an invasion force; Sudangphaa defeated it and the 1401 treaty fixed the Patkai boundary.

name: Tasim Pou Borgohain
summary: Minister who led the Mungkang invasion force for the claimant Tai Sulai.

name: Nangchukham Borgohain
summary: Sudangphaa's commander who pursued the Mungkang invaders.

name: Sujangphaa
summary: Son of Sudangphaa; died naturally.

name: Suphakphaa
summary: Son of Sujangphaa; died naturally.

name: Susenphaa
summary: Son of Suphakphaa; reigned about half a century and built a temple at Negheriting.
notes: Catalogued scenes cover a long peace and the Tangshu expedition.

name: Suhenphaa
summary: Son of Susenphaa; speared to death in his palace.
fate: Speared to death in his palace

name: Khenphung Borgohain
summary: An Ahom Borgohain in the project catalogue, ambushed by the Tangshu Nagas.

name: Supimphaa
summary: Son of Suhenphaa; died naturally. A catalogued scene shows him trying his father's killers.

name: Suhungmung (Swarganarayan)
summary: Expanded the kingdom for the first time since Sukaphaa, annexing Chutia and Dimasa territory and repelling the Bengal invasions of 1527 and 1532–33. First Ahom king to take a Hindu title, Swarganarayan.
notes: Annexed Habung 1512; Chutia kingdom 1523–24; created the Borpatragohain post 1527; killed in his sleep in 1539 by his servant Ratiman.

name: Phrasengmung Borgohain
summary: Appointed by Suhungmung to govern Sadiya after the Chutia kingdom was annexed.

name: Konseng Barpatragohain
summary: Appointed the first Borpatragohain in 1527 by Suhungmung, the year the Ahoms defeated the first Muslim invasion.

name: Bit Malik
summary: Named in the project catalogue as leading the first Muslim invasion that Suhungmung defeated in 1527.

name: Ton Kham Borgohain
summary: Defeated Turbak's invasion and pursued the invaders to the Karatoya river.

name: Turbak
summary: Led the 1532–33 invasion, defeating Suklen at Singri before the Ahoms counterattacked; killed near the Bharali river.
notes: Sources disagree on his origin (Turko-Afghan or Bengali).

name: Suklenmung (Garhgayan Roja)
summary: Made Garhgaon the capital and drove the Koch army off the north bank in 1546. In his reign Hari, Sankardev's son-in-law, was executed, leading Sankardev to leave the kingdom.
notes: Some chronicles suspected him in his father's murder.

name: Sukhaamphaa (Khora Roja)
summary: Longest-reigning Ahom king (about 51 years). Chilarai's 1563 invasion forced the Treaty of Majuli. The Ekasarana faith took firm root in his reign.
notes: Nicknamed Khora Roja after a limp from an elephant fall.

name: Aikhek Burhagohain
summary: Offered little resistance to Chilarai's 1563 invasion and was removed as Burhagohain after the Treaty of Majuli.

name: Pratap Singha (Susenghphaa)
summary: Created the Borbarua and Borphukan offices, reorganised the paik system through Momai Tamuli Borbarua, and fought the first Mughal wars.
notes: Also known as Burha Roja and Buddhiswarganarayan. Married Mangaldahi, daughter of Parikshit Narayan, in 1608.

name: Mangaldoi (Mangaldahi)
role: Koch princess, wife of Pratap Singha
summary: Daughter of Raghudev (or Parikshit Narayan in another source); married Pratap Singha to secure the alliance with Koch Hajo.

name: Momai Tamuli Borbarua
summary: Rose from humble origins to become the first Borbarua. Systematised the paik system in 1609, commanded at Duimunsila (1638) and signed the Treaty of Asurar Ali (1639). Father of Lachit Borphukan.
notes: The infobox gives 1664 and a category gives 1650 for his death.

name: Langi Panisiya
summary: First holder of the Borphukan office, based at Kajali, created under Pratap Singha.

name: Raja Satrajit of Bhusna
summary: Co-led the 1615 imperial army with Abu Bakr and stirred up Balinarayan's invasion of Kamrup.

name: Abu Bakr
summary: Co-led the 1615 imperial army that began the first Mughal attack on Assam.

name: Qasim Khan Chishti
summary: His mistreatment of hill chiefs of Dhanikal led to the Ahom asylum dispute.

name: Allah Yar Khan
summary: Signed the Treaty of Asurar Ali with Momai Tamuli in 1639, fixing the border on the Brahmaputra.

name: Suramphaa (Jayaditya Singha, Bhoga Roja)
summary: Son of Pratap Singha; deposed in 1644 and later murdered.

name: Sutingphaa (Noriya Roja)
summary: Brother of Suramphaa; deposed by the Burhagohain in 1648 and later murdered.

name: Manthir Bharali Barua (Parbatia Phukan)
summary: A Kayastha viceroy of western Assam whose appointment caused resentment among Ahom nobles.

name: Jayadhwaj Singha (Sutamla)
summary: Drove the Mughals from Guwahati in 1648. Mir Jumla took Garhgaon in March 1662; the king withdrew to Namrup and signed the Treaty of Ghilajharighat in January 1663. A patron of Vaishnava satras.
notes: Called Bhagania Roja (“the fugitive”). Struck the first coins in his name.

name: Niranjan Deva (Niranjan Bapu)
summary: Initiated Jayadhwaj Singha and was made head of Auniati Satra.

name: Atan Burhagohain
summary: Appointed Burhagohain in January 1662 while Mir Jumla held Garhgaon. Negotiated the Treaty of Ghilajharighat, commanded the northern division at Saraighat and twice declined the crown. Murdered in 1679 by men of Laluk Sola Borphukan.
notes: Served under eight kings.

name: Mir Jumla
summary: Invaded Assam in January 1662, took Garhgaon in March and agreed the Treaty of Ghilajharighat in January 1663. Died on the return at Mankachar on 30 March 1663.
notes: Born in Isfahan in 1591.

name: Dilir Khan
summary: Named in the project catalogue among the Mughal commanders of Mir Jumla's 1662 invasion.
notes: Not found in the Wikipedia articles consulted.

name: Shihabuddin Talish
summary: Chronicler of Mir Jumla's invasion of Assam.
notes: Role from the project catalogue.

name: Chakradhwaj Singha (Supangmung)
summary: Refused Mughal tribute, rebuilt the army and recaptured Guwahati in 1667. Appointed Atan Burhagohain Rajmantri Dangaria and Lachit Borphukan commander.
notes: Died April 1670.

name: Ramani Gabharu
summary: Sent to the Mughal court under the 1663 Treaty of Ghilajharighat. Sources differ on whether she was Jayadhwaj Singha's daughter or Lachit's niece.

name: Syed Firoz Khan
summary: Captured by the Ahoms and later released; carried Ram Singh's demands to the Ahom court.

name: Pakhori Gabharu
summary: Daughter of Momai Tamuli Borbarua and sister of Lachit; queen to Ahom kings.

name: Lachit Borphukan
summary: Retook Guwahati in 1667 and led the Ahom victory over a larger Mughal fleet at Saraighat in 1671. Died the next year, and his remains lie in a maidam at Jorhat.
notes: Born 24 November 1622; died 25 April 1672 at Kaliabor. Fought at Alaboi in 1669.

name: Aurangzeb
summary: Ordered Ram Singh's 1667 counter-expedition against the Ahoms.

name: Ram Singh I of Amber
summary: Led the 1667–1671 Mughal invasion of Assam; defeated at Saraighat in 1671 and demoted on his return.

name: Udayaditya Singha (Sunyatphaa)
summary: Brother of Chakradhwaj; renewed the war with the Mughals and ordered Lachit to Saraighat. Deposed and executed.

name: Munawar Khan
summary: Named among the Mughal commanders at Saraighat.

name: Ramdhwaj Singha (Suklamphaa)
summary: Brother of Udayaditya; poisoned in 1674 during court intrigue.

name: Laluk Sola Borphukan
summary: Elder brother of Lachit; succeeded him as Borphukan. Handed Guwahati to the Mughals in 1679 and was assassinated by his bodyguard in 1680.
notes: Wikipedia dates his tenure 1672–1677 and his death 1680.

name: Debera Borbarua
summary: Dominated the court in the 1672–1675 succession struggle, setting up the short-lived kings Suhung and Gobar Roja.
notes: From the project catalogue only; check against the Buranjis.

name: Suhung (Samaguria Roja)
summary: Raised to the throne by Debera Borbarua and deposed after about 21 days.

name: Gobar Roja
summary: A puppet king under Debera Borbarua, deposed and executed after about 24 days.
notes: Father of Gadadhar Singha.
fate: Deposed and executed after about 24 days

name: Sujinphaa (Arjun Konwar)
summary: Grandson of Pratap Singha, installed by Atan Burhagohain; deposed and died by suicide.

name: Sudoiphaa (Parvatia Roja)
summary: King during the 1679 conspiracy that led to the murder of Atan Burhagohain; deposed and killed.

name: Joymoti Konwari
role: Ahom princess and wife of Gadadhar Singha
summary: Wife of the prince who became king Gadadhar Singha. Tortured and killed by agents of Sulikphaa and Laluk Sola Borphukan while her husband hid in exile.

name: Sulikphaa (Ratnadhwaj Singha, Lora Roja)
summary: A boy king under Laluk Sola Borphukan; deposed and killed. A rule that claimants must be physically unblemished was introduced in his reign.

name: Muhammad Azam Shah
summary: Invited in 1679 to take the Saraighat fort after Laluk Sola's surrender.

name: Gadadhar Singha (Supaatphaa)
summary: Founder of the Tungkhungia line. Came out of exile in the Naga hills to take the throne in 1681 and retook Guwahati at Itakhuli in 1682, ending the Ahom–Mughal wars.
notes: Husband of Joymoti Konwari. Built the Dhodar Ali road and began a land survey.
relation: Son of Gobar Roja; first Tungkhungia king

name: Rudra Singha (Sukhrungphaa)
summary: Took the kingdom to its peak, founded Rangpur as the capital, campaigned against the Dimasa and Jaintia kingdoms (1706–08) and planned a great war on Mughal Bengal, dying before it began.
notes: Born c. 1665; died 27 August 1714 at North Guwahati.

name: Krishnaram Bhattacharya Nyayavagish
summary: A scholar from Nabadwip invited as religious guide under Rudra Singha; later adviser (Parbatiya Gosain) under Siva Singha.

name: Ghanashyam Khanikar
summary: Named in the project catalogue as the architect behind Rudra Singha's building of Rangpur.
notes: Not found in the Rudra Singha article; treat as unverified.

name: Siva Singha (Sutanphaa)
summary: A devout Shakta who gave land to temples and Brahmins and shared royal authority with his queens, who ruled in turn as Bar Raja. A golden age of Assamese manuscripts.

name: Phuleswari (Pramatheswari)
role: Queen who ruled as Bar Raja
summary: A dancer of the Nat caste made Bar Raja under Siva Singha after astrologers predicted the king's fall. Minted coins in joint names and pressed to make Shaktism the state religion; died in 1731 in childbirth.
notes: Her insult to the Moamoria Gosains is cited as a cause of the later rebellion.

name: Ambika
role: Queen who ruled as Bar Raja
summary: Phuleswari's sister. Sponsored the Hastividyarnava and the Sivasagar Siva Doul.
notes: Sources give her death as 1738 or the end of her reign as 1739.

name: Sarbeswari (Endari)
role: Queen who ruled as Bar Raja
summary: Held the same authority as her predecessors but was less active in patronising Shaktism.

name: Pramatta Singha (Sunenphaa)
summary: Brother of Siva Singha; died naturally. Catalogued scenes show Rang Ghar games in his reign.

name: Rajeswar Singha (Suremphaa)
summary: Fourth son of Rudra Singha. Sheltered Bhagyachandra of Manipur, sent the failed 1765 expedition, and married Kuranganayani in 1768. Much of the governing fell to Kirti Chandra Borbarua.
notes: Died at Dergaon in 1769. Added three underground storeys to the Kareng Ghar (Talatal Ghar).

name: Kirti Chandra Borbarua (Gendhela)
summary: Held real power under Rajeswar Singha and made Lakshmi Singha king in 1769. Had the Buranjis collected and many destroyed over references to his low origins.

name: Haranath Bitarual Phukan
summary: Led the 1765 army sent to help Manipur against the Burmese; the jungle route defeated it and it became known as the War of the Creepers.

name: Kuranganayani
role: Manipuri princess, queen of the Ahom kingdom
summary: Married Rajeswar Singha in 1768 as thanks for Ahom help to her father. After his death she was taken by the rebel Ragha Moran and helped bring about his killing in April 1770; she later married Lakshmi Singha.

name: Lakshmi Singha (Sunyeophaa)
summary: Made king by Kirti Chandra Borbarua. The Moamoria rebellion began in 1769 and the rebels captured him; royalists restored him in 1770.
notes: Died 13 December 1780.

name: Mayamara Mahanta
summary: Intervened to spare Lakshmi Singha's life when the rebels captured him in 1769.

name: Ragha Neog (Raghab Borbarua)
summary: Flogged over elephant levies in September 1769, which sparked the revolt. Became Borbarua and was killed in April 1770 by nobles aided by Kuranganayani.

name: Naharkhora Saikia
summary: Co-leader with Ragha; helped install his son Ramakanta as rebel king and was executed in the 1770 purge.

name: Ramakanta
summary: Naharkhora's son, placed on the throne by the rebels in November 1769 and executed in 1770.

name: Gaurinath Singha (Suhitpangphaa)
summary: Became king at about fifteen. Rebels took the capital in 1786; British troops under Captain Welsh restored order in lower Assam in 1792–94 and then left. Died at Jorhat in December 1794.
notes: The infobox gives 1794 as the end; the king list gives 1795.

name: Harihar Tanti
summary: Reorganised the Dafla-Bhatia rebels in 1786 and administered the north bank of the Brahmaputra.

name: Bharat Singha
summary: Moamoria chief placed on the throne after the 1785–86 rebel victory; coins were struck in his name. Killed in 1799 (another page gives 1800).

name: Captain Thomas Welsh
summary: Led the British contingent that took Guwahati in 1792 and Rangpur in March 1794; recalled in April 1794.

name: Lord Cornwallis
summary: Ordered the dispatch of Captain Welsh's troops to Assam.

name: Kamaleswar Singha (Suklingphaa)
summary: Placed on the throne as an infant by Purnananda Burhagohain, who held real power; died of smallpox.

name: Purnananda Burhagohain
summary: Placed Kamaleswar and then Chandrakanta on the throne and ran the state for two decades. Collapsed and died on 27 March 1817 on learning that Badan Chandra Borphukan was with the Burmese.
notes: His eldest son Ruchinath succeeded him as Burhagohain.

name: Sarbananda Singha
role: Rebel ruler of the Moran tracts
summary: Ruled the Moran tracts from Bengmara. After fighting royalists in 1805 he accepted peace, became Barsenapati and governed the autonomous Matak kingdom.

name: Chandrakanta Singha (Sudingphaa)
summary: Named king at about fourteen by Purnananda Burhagohain. Deposed in 1818, reinstalled by the Burmese in 1819, defeated in 1822 and fled to British territory. Died in Guwahati in 1839.
notes: Born c. 1797. After Yandabo he received a pension of 500 rupees.

name: Badan Chandra Borphukan
summary: Went to the Burmese court in 1816 seeking help against Purnananda Burhagohain and returned with an army in 1817. Assassinated by Subedar Rup Singh.
notes: Sources give 1817 or 1818 for the assassination; the Wikipedia article gives 1818.

name: Bodawpaya
summary: Received Badan Chandra Borphukan in 1816 and sent the first Burmese expedition into Assam in 1817.

name: Numali Rajmao
summary: Reportedly behind the plot that led to the murder of Badan Chandra Borphukan.

name: Ruchinath Burhagohain
summary: Eldest son of Purnananda; became Burhagohain in 1817, deposed Chandrakanta in February 1818 and installed Purandar Singha, and later sought British help.

name: Purandar Singha
summary: Installed as a boy in 1818 by Ruchinath Burhagohain, lost the throne to the Burmese in 1819, and was made a tributary prince by the British in 1833. Deposed in September 1838.
notes: Born 1807, died 1 October 1846 at Jorhat. Also called Suremphaa II.

name: Subedar Rup Singh
summary: Killed Badan Chandra Borphukan, in a plot backed by the queen-mother.

name: Kiamingi (Ala Mingi)
summary: Commanded Bodawpaya's second invasion in 1819; after the Burmese victory he reinstalled Chandrakanta Singha.

name: Jogeswar Singha
summary: A puppet king installed by the Burmese commander Mingimaha Tilwa in 1821; removed in 1822.

name: Mingimaha Tilwa
summary: Sent to Assam in 1821; installed Jogeswar Singha, defeated Chandrakanta in June 1822 and was declared Raja of Assam, ending Ahom rule.

name: Bagyidaw
summary: Sent Mingimaha Tilwa to Assam in 1821 and ruled through the First Anglo-Burmese War.

name: Maha Bandula
summary: Led 20,000 men to defeat Chandrakanta in 1822; killed at Danubyu in the First Anglo-Burmese War.

name: David Scott
role: British Agent on the north-east frontier
summary: British official in Assam and the north-east in the years before and after Yandabo.
notes: Role from general knowledge; check against a dedicated source.

name: Colonel Alfred Richards
summary: Named in the project catalogue in the First Anglo-Burmese War scenes.

name: Sir Archibald Campbell
summary: Led the 1824 Yangon expedition and co-signed the Treaty of Yandabo on 24 February 1826.

name: Bhopal (Kachari, traditional list)
summary: Named in a popular king list as a Kachari ruler of the 13th–14th century; not found in the scholarly sources reviewed.
notes: Treat as unverified.

name: Purandar (Kachari, traditional list)
summary: Named in the same popular king list; unverified.
notes: Not the Ahom king Purandar Singha.

name: Mahamanikya (Barahi king)
role: Barahi (Kachari) king of the Kapili valley
summary: Ruled around Nagaon, Morigaon and Hojai; patron of the poet Madhava Kandali. A Hojai (Lanka) inscription dated 1352 records a land grant; some historians say he joined Kamata and the Bhuyans against Sikandar Shah around 1362.
notes: Called Borahi-Kachari king Manikpha in one source; the lineage label varies.

name: Bicharpatiha (Prakash, traditional list)
summary: The same list places him at Dimapur from 1336; the Dimasa Kingdom article says early king lists are late constructions and should be treated with caution.
notes: Treat as unverified.

name: Nandi (Nandisvara)
summary: Ruled from Sadhayapura (Sadiya); known from a grant issued by his son Satyanarayana, who also names his mother Daivaki.

name: Satyanarayana (Ratnanarayana)
summary: Son of Nandi; ruled from Sadhayapura. A later Chutia king names Ratnanarayana, identified with him, as king of Kamatapura, which may show a link between Sadiya and Kamata.
notes: The Ratnanarayana identification is a scholarly suggestion.

name: Lakshminarayana (Dharmanarayana)
summary: Chutia king known from sources dated 1392 and 1401.

name: Durlabhnarayana (Chutia)
summary: Chutia king known from a grant dated 1428.
notes: Not the Kamata king of the same name.

name: Muktadharmanarayana
summary: Known from an inscription dated 1442.

name: Pratyaksanarayana (Yasanarayana)
summary: Chutia king known without dates; the page notes a possible match with Yasanarayana of the Dhenukhana plate.

name: Yasamanarayana
summary: Chutia king of the late 15th century; may be the Yasanarayana of the Dhenukhana plate.

name: Purandarnarayana
summary: Chutia king listed before Dhirnarayan; no events are given.

name: Dhirnarayan
summary: Built a fort at Dikhowmukh in 1513, was routed attacking the Ahom fort at Dibru in 1523, and was killed, ending the kingdom in 1523–24.
notes: Known from an inscription dated 1522.

name: Khorapha
summary: Issued a silver coin in 1520 and was killed in an Ahom attack in 1526.

name: Kasitora
summary: A minister said to have been defeated alongside Dhirnarayan.

name: Sadhaknarayan
summary: Prince after the fall; accounts differ on whether he was deported to Darrang or killed.

name: Khunkhara
summary: Succeeded his brother Khorapha and fled Dimapur when the Ahoms attacked in 1531.

name: Detsung (Dersung)
summary: Installed by Suhungmung, to whom he gave his sister in marriage; killed when he tried to break free. The Ahoms occupied Dimapur in 1536.

name: Yasho Narayan (Satrudaman)
summary: Ruled North Cachar, the Dhansiri valley and parts of Sylhet and struck coins in his name.

name: Jasa Manik
summary: Jaintia king whose manoeuvres are linked to the Dimasa–Ahom conflict of 1618.

name: Ram Singh I (Jaintia)
summary: Kidnapped the Dimasa king, prompting Rudra Singha's 1707–08 invasion; died an Ahom captive.

name: Tamradhwaj Narayan
summary: Declared independence; Rudra Singha invaded Maibong in December 1706 and destroyed its fort. Tamradhwaj fled to Jaintia and was imprisoned.

name: Bhagyachandra (Jai Singh)
summary: Fled to Ahom territory after the Burmese invasion of 1764 and was sheltered by Rajeswar Singha, who backed his return; reinstated in 1773. Promoted Vaishnavism and the Manipuri Raas Leela.

name: Krishnachandra Narayan
summary: Sheltered Moamoria rebels, causing Ahom–Dimasa skirmishes from 1803 to 1805; helped Manipur against the Burmese.

name: Ram Singh II (Jaintia)
summary: Long-reigning Jaintia king who agreed in 1824 to deal only with the British.

name: Govindachandra Narayan
summary: Restored by the British after the 1826 Treaty of Yandabo; died in 1830.
notes: The two sources split his reign into two periods.

name: Gambhir Singha
summary: Repulsed the Burmese in 1825.

name: Birpal (legendary)
summary: Figure of the Chutiyar Rajar Vamsavali (published 1850), a late manuscript that scholars treat as legendary; historians think it was composed in the early 19th century.
notes: No historical standing; included because it appears in popular lists.

name: Hema Saraswati
summary: Counted among the first known Assamese writers, patron Durlabhnarayan. His Prahlada Charita is regarded as the earliest known Assamese poem.
notes: No explicit dates in the source.

name: Harihara Vipra
summary: Pre-Vaishnava Assamese poet; wrote Babruvahanar Yuddha.
notes: Century from a category tag only.

name: Madhava Kandali
summary: Author of the Saptakanda Ramayana, regarded as the oldest rendering of the Ramayana into an Indo-Aryan language. Patron: Mahamanikya, a Kachari king.
notes: Dated by a stone inscription equated with 1352.

name: Srimanta Sankardev
summary: Founder of the Ekasarana bhakti movement and a defining figure of Assamese literature, music and dance. Wrote the Kirtana-ghosha, borgeets and Ankia Naat plays.
notes: Scholars give his death as 1569. Wives: Suryava and Kalindi; son Ramananda.

notes: Dates from memory of standard accounts; verify.

name: Bhattadev
summary: Prose translator of the Bhagavata and Gita (Katha Bhagavata, Katha Gita); head of Patbausi satra and founder of Byaskuchi satra.

summary: Assamese entrepreneur who pioneered tea planting and was hanged for his part in the 1857 revolt.

summary: Chief Minister of Assam from 1950 to 1957.

name: The Pala line of Kamarupa ends
summary: Jaya Pala is the last known king of the Pala line. The name Kamarupa fades over the next century as the old kingdom breaks into regions (the end is variously dated 1100, 1140 or the 13th century).

name: Bengal's Palas take western Kamarupa
summary: Ramapala conquers the west and puts Timgyadeva in charge (c. 1110–1126). Vaidyadeva follows (c. 1126–1140) and in effect founds a separate kingdom after Kumarapala's death.

name: A “lunar dynasty” on the north bank
summary: Bhaskara, Rayarideva, Udayakarna and Vallabhadeva hold parts of Kamrup, Darrang and Sonitpur. They are known from a single 1185 inscription.

name: Bakhtiyar Khalji's army is destroyed
summary: On his way back from a failed Tibet campaign, Bakhtiyar's army is annihilated in Kamarupa. The king who defeated him is traditionally called Prithu, but that identification is disputed.

name: Iwaz Khalji and Nasiruddin Mahmud
summary: Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Khalji invades and withdraws; he is captured and killed in 1227–28. Nasiruddin Mahmud installs a tributary king in Kamarupa who loses control after 1229.

name: Sukaphaa reaches Assam
summary: After leaving Mong Mao in 1215, Sukaphaa arrives at Namrup in December 1228. The Ahom kingdom is dated from here. In the west, Sandhya takes the throne of Kamarupa in the same year.

name: Yuzbak is defeated; Kamata takes shape
summary: Ikhtiyaruddin Yuzbak, governor of Bengal, invades and is defeated and killed or captured by Sandhya. Sandhya moves the capital to Kamatapur, founding the Kamata kingdom.

name: Bahadur Shah raids Kamata
summary: Ghiyasuddin Bahadur Shah of Sonargaon raids as far as Nagaon, meeting ineffective resistance from Pratapdhwaj and the Kacharis, but keeps no territory.

name: The first Ahom–Kamata war
summary: A long war between Sukhaangphaa and the Kamata king ends in a truce. It is sealed by Sukhaangphaa's marriage to the Kamata princesses Rajani and Bhajani.

name: Mahamanikya and the Saptakanda Ramayana
summary: The Barahi king Mahamanikya rules around Nagaon and Hojai (a 1352 inscription records his grant) and sponsors Madhava Kandali's Ramayana.

name: Durlabhnarayan's court poets
summary: Under Durlabhnarayan of Kamata, poets such as Hema Saraswati and Harihara Vipra write some of the earliest Assamese literature.

name: Ilyas Shah and Sikandar Shah invade
summary: Bengal forces occupy Kamrup including Guwahati in 1356–57. Sikandar Shah then pushes to the Kopili, where Kamata, Bhuyan and Barahi forces fight him near Gachtal. A coin of 1360 carries a Kamrup mint name.

name: The Chutia kingdom appears in the record
summary: Nandi and Satyanarayana rule from Sadhayapura (Sadiya), the earliest Chutia kings known from inscriptions. Tyao Khamti's expedition against them fails (1380–87).

name: Interregnums in the Ahom kingdom
summary: Three Ahom kings are assassinated or die, and the throne stays empty for long stretches (1364–1369, 1376–1380, 1389–1397).

name: Sudangphaa restores the Ahom throne
summary: The prince raised by a Brahmin family in Habung is found and enthroned in 1397. A 1401 treaty fixes the Patkai boundary and in 1403 the capital moves to Charguwa.

name: Kamata and the Ahoms drive back Azam Shah
summary: The Kamata king, allied with Sudangphaa by marriage, expels Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah across the Karatoya. A Boko inscription shows the Sultanate held part of Kamrup for some years.

name: Bhuyan rule in Kamata
summary: After Indranarayan, the Bhuyan Arimatta seizes the throne, followed by Gajanka, Sukranka and Mriganka (dates are reconstructed).

name: The Khen dynasty
summary: Niladhwaj (1440–1460), Chakradhwaj (1460–1480) and Nilambar (1480–1498) rule from Kamatapur. Nilambar expands the kingdom into Kamrup and Darrang.

name: Two Ahom kings in quick succession
summary: Suhenphaa is speared to death in his palace in 1493; Supimphaa rules until 1497, when Suhungmung takes the throne.

name: Muzaffar Shah takes parts of Kamata
summary: The Bengal sultan conquers part of Kamata and issues coins with the title Kamata Mardan.

name: Husain Shah conquers Kamata
summary: Shah Ismail Ghazi besieges and destroys Kamatapur and captures Nilambar, ending the Khen dynasty. The Sultanate holds land up to Hajo by 1502. Dates of the conquest vary between 1498 and 1499.

name: The Bhuyans end Sultanate rule
summary: Under Harup Narayan the Assamese Bhuyans overrun Danyal's garrison about ten years after the conquest. Rule passes to the Bhuyans until the Koch rise.

name: Suhungmung annexes the Chutia kingdom
summary: Habung is taken in 1512 and Dhirnarayan is routed at Dibru in 1523. By 1524 Phrasengmung Borgohain governs Sadiya.

name: Biswa Singha founds the Koch kingdom
summary: Biswa Singha is crowned in Kamata after defeating the Baro-Bhuyans, ending the confusing interval of fragments left after the Khen.

name: Sukaphaa Departs Mong Mao
summary: Prince Sukaphaa leaves his ancestral kingdom of Mong Mao following a succession dispute, leading 9,000 followers, noblemen, priests (Deodhais), horses, and two royal war elephants across Upper Burma towards Assam.

name: Sukaphaa Departs Mong Mao
summary: Prince Sukaphaa leaves his ancestral kingdom of Mong Mao following a succession dispute, leading 9,000 followers, noblemen, priests (Deodhais), horses, and two royal war elephants across Upper Burma towards Assam.
